content: Listeriosis is a group of infectious diseases caused by bacteria from the genus Listeria, most commonly Listeria monocytogenes. This bacterium is a flagellated, catalase-positive, facultative intracellular, anaerobic, Gram-positive bacillus. The infection is relatively rare, with an annual incidence in the United States of approximately 0.2 to 0.3 cases per 100,000 individuals. Transmission typically occurs through the consumption of contaminated food or via vertical transmission from a pregnant mother to her fetus. Once inside the human host, Listeria monocytogenes expresses thermoregulated virulence factors, invades the intestinal epithelium, and multiplies intracellularly within phagocytic phagolysosomes. The bacterium can escape lysosomal destruction by secreting phospholipases and listeriolysin O, a hemolysin that disrupts the vacuole membrane. It spreads between cells by forming actin-based protrusions, known as filopods or rockets, which facilitate cell-to-cell migration. Microscopically, infected tissues often show inflammation, exudate formation, and neutrophilia. In chronic infections, macrophages may accumulate, and granulomas may form. The clinical manifestations of listeriosis are diverse and include neonatal listeriosis, genitourinary infections, gastroenteritis, central nervous system (CNS) infections, endocarditis, bacteremia, and localized infections. Risk factors for developing listeriosis include the consumption of uncooked meats, unpasteurized dairy products, processed or ready-to-eat meats, and smoked seafood. Populations at higher risk include immunosuppressed individuals (e.g., transplant recipients, patients with splenectomy, those on immunosuppressive therapy, or those with advanced diabetes, kidney or liver disease, or active malignancy), neonates, pregnant women, and the elderly. In healthy individuals, listeriosis often causes no symptoms or only mild, transient bacteremia. If untreated, the disease can progress over 1 to 90 days, leading to complications such as bacteremia, abscess formation, pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute kidney injury, and CNS involvement. Healthy children and young adults generally have a good prognosis, but high-risk populations are more likely to experience severe complications or death, even with prompt treatment. The diagnosis of listeriosis is confirmed by isolating Listeria monocytogenes from a normally sterile site, such as blood, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), or amniotic fluid/placenta. Cultures from non-sterile sites, such as stool, are not routinely recommended but may be useful in cases of suspected gastroenteritis. Since Listeria is an intracellular organism, Gram staining is often unreliable, and selective enrichment media may be required to improve detection rates. CSF analysis can confirm CNS involvement, and brain MRI may reveal characteristic lesions in the cerebellum, brainstem, or cortex. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for the Listeria HLY gene is diagnostic but not widely available. Serological tests, such as listeriolysin O titers, are controversial and not recommended. Treatment for listeriosis requires antibiotic therapy. Ampicillin, with or without gentamicin, is the first-line treatment. For patients allergic to penicillins, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is an alternative. The duration of therapy depends on the clinical syndrome, ranging from a few days for uncomplicated gastroenteritis to six weeks for endocarditis or encephalitis. Listerial gastroenteritis is often self-limiting in healthy adults, but a short course of oral ampicillin may be considered for immunocompromised or pregnant individuals or those exposed to contaminated food during outbreaks. Non-gastrointestinal listeriosis typically requires hospitalization and intravenous antibiotics. Surgery is rarely needed but may be indicated for complications such as abscess drainage or valve repair in advanced endocarditis. Preventing listeriosis involves proper food handling, thorough cooking of meat and poultry, safe food storage, and maintaining a clean kitchen environment. High-risk individuals, such as pregnant women, the elderly, and immunocompromised patients, should take additional precautions, such as avoiding unpasteurized dairy products and certain ready-to-eat foods. There is no vaccine for listeriosis, and pharmacologic prophylaxis is not recommended. Historically, Listeria monocytogenes was first isolated in 1926 by Everitt Murray and was initially described as a pathogen of laboratory animals. The first human cases were reported in 1929 by Nyfeldt in Denmark. The bacterium was renamed in 1940 to honor Joseph Lister. Listeriosis has a global distribution, affecting both developed and developing countries, with higher incidence rates among pregnant women, neonates, the elderly, and Hispanic populations.
